title: Mesh-shard latency scratchpad
body:
Purpose:
Quick working notes from a set of small experiments aimed at understanding how non-uniform GPU mesh placement and randomised NIC/PCIe perturbations affect tail latency for our shard+pipeline inference configurations. Goal is to surface simple heuristics we can add to the scheduler (placement scoring) to reduce 95/99p regressions for medium-length sequences (512-1024 tokens).

Background/context (why this felt necessary):
- We've seen intermittent 95/99p regressions for certain tenants using shard-based models (tp+pp mixes). Hard to reproduce with standard per-node microbenchmarks.
- Theory: small mismatches in on-host peer-to-peer paths + host staging variability create asymmetric transfer windows that blow up tail when combined with pipelined compute skews.
- This is a working, informal capture — not a full paper.

Experimental setup (short):
- Model: 13B transformer, token length 512 / 1024, kv-cache on host for warm prefixes.
- Topologies evaluated: "compact" (all shards on same nvlink island), "spread-rack" (across two hosts same rack), "cross-rack" (across two racks via TOR), "mesh-mixed" (1 shard on local host, others distributed across 3 hosts).
- Sharding: 4-way tensor parallel across GPUs; pipeline stages 2 per GPU (micro-batched pipeline).
- Workload: synthetic QPS ramp: 0 -> 200 qps over 5 minutes, steady-state 200 qps for 10 minutes, then 400 qps sudden burst. Repeat 3 times.
- Instrumentation: per-GPU ts, host NIC counters, PCIe stall counters, custom tracepoint at kv-cache hit/miss. Collect per-request timeline (send, host-staging, p2p, compute start/end, reply).

Run notes (chronological):
2025-09-22 09:00: baseline compact run
- 95p: 18.2 ms, 99p: 32.7 ms. Very stable.
- kv-cache hit ratio 94% at steady state.

2025-09-22 10:15: spread-rack (two hosts same rack, each with NVLink partial connectivity)
- 95p: 24.6 ms, 99p: 48.9 ms. Increased tail and higher variance.
- Observed short bursts of host-side PCIe queues (seen via PCIe TX queue depth spikes) correlating with 99p.

2025-09-22 11:30: cross-rack (TOR, 25 Gbps constrained route simulated)
- 95p: 46.1 ms, 99p: 120.3 ms. Extremely sensitive to small packet serialization delays.
- NIC retransmit counters ticked during burst; suggests buffer pressure and backpressure cascades.

2025-09-23 14:00: mesh-mixed with host-level NIC shaping (random 0-5% packet drop + 1-3ms jitter)
- 95p: 60-95 ms (flaky across runs), 99p: spikes > 300 ms on some bursts.
- Key observation: when a single pipeline stage is placed on a host with jittered NIC, downstream pipeline stages experience queue build-up; because we use strict ordering semantics for sequence tokens, the whole request stalls at the slowest hop.

Micro-insights (what looks important):
- Nonlinear amplification: a ~2-3 ms average added on one link can multiply to 50-200 ms 99p depending on which pipeline stage it hit. The nonlinearity increases with deeper pipelines and lower batch sizes.
- Host-staging and PCIe stalls are as important as interconnect bandwidth when host is responsible for KV cache reads. Host staging variability + PCIe queueing often precedes NIC retransmits in the failure timeline.
- KV-cache misses (or cold prefixes) show disproportionately worse tails under spread topologies.

Quick reproducible commands (approx):
- workload generator: ./bench/bench_runner --model 13B --seq 512 --qps-profile ramp-0-200-400.json --kv-host-cache yes --prefix-warm 1000
- topology injection helper (run on nodes): sudo tc qdisc add dev eth0 root netem delay 2ms 1ms distribution normal loss 0.5%
- PCIe tracing (root): echo 1 > /sys/kernel/debug/pcie_stall_trace/enable && cat /sys/kernel/debug/pcie_stall_trace/log > pcie-log.txt

Hypotheses to validate next (short list):
1) Placement sensitivity heuristic: avoid placing the first pipeline stage (the stage that touches host-kv most) on nodes that are not NVLink-local to the largest compute shard. Score candidate nodes by host-kv-to-gpu-pcie latency and prefer compact placement if score delta > threshold.
2) Small jitter amplification test: add micro-jitter (0.5-2ms) to different hops to map where multiplicative amplification occurs (we only injected at NIC in current runs).
3) Backpressure smoothing: experiment with permissive re-ordering / small token-level prefetch to decouple strict per-token blocking at the pipeline boundaries. Might reduce extreme tails at the cost of memory.
4) Host staging priority: give higher cgroup/netprio to host-kv read threads during burst windows to lower PCIe stall probability.

Preliminary scheduler heuristic (sketch):
- For each placement candidate, compute score = alpha*(avg_host_pcie_latency) + beta*(nvlink_bandwidth_locality_score) + gamma*(rack_boundary_penalty). For alpha/beta/gamma tuned via grid search on a small validation set. If score(compact) - score(spread) > X, choose compact.

Open questions and measurement gaps:
- We lack fine-grained cross-layer traces for packet-level re-order events at TOR + switch queue depths. Need to ask infra to dump switch stats during next run.
- How do quantization-driven compute skews interact? We tested mostly fp16; run plan to include int8 pathways where compute time per-layer changes.
- TTL of the heuristic: will it hurt utilization for DL batch workloads? Need to run joint scheduler simulations.

Next actions (TODOs):
- [ ] Run focused jitter injection on PCIe host staging path (not just NIC). Time budget 2 days (Ben).
- [ ] Add int8 path to the bench and re-run mesh-mixed configuration (Maya).
- [ ] Draft a thin scheduler PR prototype with scoring function and unit-tests against historical traces (Aisha + Ethan).
- [ ] Ask infra for TOR switch queue dumps (JIRA INF-879).

Notes for a future public writeup (if we generalize):
- Emphasize the "amplifier" effect: small link perturbations become large tail effects when combined with ordering constraints in pipeline + kv-host semantics.
- Provide simple placement rules that are low-cost to compute and integrate into existing allocator.

Appendix: short example timeline snippet (single request)
- t0 request enqueue at ingress layer
- t1 host staging read (kv hit) start (local host)
- t1.8 host staging completes, PCIe transfer to GPU begins
- t2 GPU0 compute start (time jitter +/- 0.8ms)
- t2.9 GPU0 compute end, p2p to GPU1 (cross-host) starts
- t3.3 p2p delayed by 1-2ms (NIC jitter) -> GPU1 compute start delayed -> pipeline queue builds -> eventually request completion delayed by 80ms

If you want to repro one of the bad runs exactly, talk to me for the exact bench artifacts (I left the run directory on bench-vm-07: /mnt/bench/runs/mesh-2025-09-23-14h).

Informal closing:
This felt productive — the pattern that small link/host perturbations can explode in tails is consistent across different synthetic profiles. The immediate value is a simple placement avoidance rule for the "first stage" of the pipeline and a short experiment to test small reordering (prefetch) to break strict per-token blocking.

-- Aisha
